title: Documentation, Result Reporting, and Quality Assurance

sections.learningObjectives:
- Document and report waived-test results accurately, completely, legibly, and at the time of testing, including the required identifying and traceability elements.
- Perform and support quality assurance activities, including quality control, logging, monitoring, and corrective action, within the assistant's scope.
- Maintain accurate test, quality control, and temperature logs without falsifying, backdating, or altering entries.
- Escalate unusual, invalid, or critical results and quality problems to licensed staff or supervisors per office policy.
- Recognize scope-of-practice boundaries by reporting and documenting results rather than interpreting or diagnosing them.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

It is like writing down a phone number the moment someone tells it to you, before you forget it. You write the test answer right away so it does not get lost or mixed up.

### Question 2

Imagine keeping score in a game: if you wait until the game is over to write the points, you might forget some. Writing the answer down right away keeps the score correct.

### Question 3

It is like getting a delivery at your door while you are writing down an important number: finish writing the number first, then open the door.

### Question 4

A good test note is like a complete address on an envelope: it says who it is about, when it happened, who did it, and what the answer was.

### Question 5

Quality assurance is like a coach who watches the whole team all season to help everyone play safely and well, not someone who only shows up after a big mistake.

### Question 6

Quality control is like checking your scale against a known weight before you weigh yourself. Quality assurance is the bigger plan that also makes sure the scale is stored well and checked on schedule.

### Question 7

If the fridge thermometer shows your milk got too warm, you would not just cross out the number and pretend it was cold. You would tell an adult and check whether the milk is still safe.

### Question 8

A QC log is like a science notebook: it writes down what you tested, when, with which batch, and who did it, so you can check the work later.

### Question 9

It is like a referee writing down the score: the referee writes what actually happened, and the coach decides what it means. The assistant writes the real answer and lets the provider sort out the worry.

### Question 10

Test results are like a report card that goes to the teacher first, not to everyone in the hallway. The provider gets the result and then talks to the patient.

### Question 11

If a friend asks you what a strange shadow on an X-ray means, you would say 'the doctor will explain it' rather than guessing. The assistant points the question to the provider.

### Question 12

If you make a mistake in a notebook, you draw one line through it and write the fix next to it with your name, so everyone can still see what happened. You do not scribble it out completely.

### Question 13

If you write a note to your future self that you cannot read later, it does not help. Test notes must be clear so anyone can read the answer later.

### Question 14

When you open a new box of cookies, you check the date and note which batch it is. A new test lot gets the same check so you always know which batch you used.

### Question 15

Escalate is like telling a teacher when something is too big for you to handle. You pass it to the person who has the training and authority to fix it.

### Question 16

If your scale shows a known 10-pound weight as 20 pounds, you would not weigh yourself and guess. You would fix the scale first and tell someone it is broken.

### Question 17

The control line is like the 'power on' light of a toy. If the light never turns on, the toy is not working, and you cannot trust anything it does.

### Question 18

A waived test is like an easy recipe: it is simple, but you still follow the recipe and write down what you made. Easy does not mean no notes.

### Question 19

A ruler says the line is at 4.3 centimeters; you write 4.3, not 'about 4.' The assistant writes the exact answer the test shows.

### Question 20

The person who bakes the cookies is the one who knows what went in them. The person who runs the test writes down what they saw.

### Question 21

You cannot write a book report for a book you did not read. The person who did the test writes the result, because they actually saw it.

### Question 22

You would not write 'the cake is done' before you bake it. Writing a test answer before the test happens is guessing, and guessing is dangerous in medicine.

### Question 23

Before you put a name on a test, you check two things that belong only to that person, like their name and birthday, so the answer goes to the right person.

### Question 24

Logs are like a class attendance sheet: they keep a real record of what happened and when, so nothing can be quietly forgotten.

### Question 25

If you hand a note to your teacher, you might say 'I gave it to Ms. Lee at 2 o'clock.' Writing that down proves the note was delivered.

### Question 26

The assistant is like the scorekeeper who writes the points and hands them to the coach; the coach decides what the score means and what to do next.

### Question 27

QC is checking one light bulb to see if it works; QA is looking after the whole string of lights so they all keep working.

### Question 28

If milk sat out all night, you would not just shove it back in the fridge and pour it into cereal. You would set it aside and ask an adult whether it is still safe.

### Question 29

If your ruler is bent, measuring the table with it still gives a wrong number, even if the number looks fine. You fix the ruler before you trust any measurement.

### Question 30

You check the smoke alarm battery on schedule even on busy weeks, because the check is what tells you the alarm will actually warn you.

### Question 31

If a toy starts beeping in a way you have never heard, you stop and check the instructions or ask an adult, instead of smashing every button.

### Question 32

You would not use expired milk to check whether your cereal is good. The check only works if the checking ingredient is fresh.

### Question 33

If you keep tripping on a loose rug, corrective action is fixing the rug, not blaming your feet. You fix the cause so it does not happen again.

### Question 34

If many cookies from the same batch come out burned, you tell the grown-up so they can check the oven, instead of quietly throwing the cookies away.

### Question 35

It is like a coach re-checking that players still know the plays each season, so the team keeps playing safely.

### Question 36

When a new delivery of baking mix arrives, you check the date, write down which batch it is, and make one test batch before serving guests.

### Question 37

It is like keeping the batch number on a bag of snacks so that if one bag is bad, the store can pull the whole batch off the shelf.

### Question 38

If a measuring cup says one cup but the bowl looks nearly empty, you check the cup and the steps, and tell the grown-up, rather than rewriting the number.

### Question 39

A critical value is like a fire alarm going off: it means act now and tell the person in charge right away.

### Question 40

If the main teacher is out and the fire alarm rings, you find the next adult in charge and keep going until someone helps.

### Question 41

Results are like a sealed report card: the office has rules about who may open and share it, and you follow those rules instead of handing it to whoever asks.

### Question 42

Some papers are like a secret: you would not leave them on a table where everyone walking by can read them.

### Question 43

If you spill water on your homework, you do not throw it out or rewrite it from memory; you show the teacher and fix it the way the rules say.

### Question 44

It is like repeating a phone number back to the person who gave it to you, so they can say 'yes, that is right.'

### Question 45

Writing '3 o'clock' one day and '15:00' the next is confusing, like mixing two languages. You pick one way and use it every time.

### Question 46

Saying 'there is sugar' means something very different if you are talking about a cup of juice versus a cup of salt water. You have to say which liquid you tested.

### Question 47

If two classmates have nearly the same name, you check their full name and birthday before handing back the right paper.

### Question 48

It is like keeping score in a game so you can tell if the team is getting better, instead of just hoping it is.

### Question 49

If a whole class forgets to write their names on papers, the teacher re-teaches the rule and checks again, instead of throwing the papers away.

### Question 50

It is like trying a new way to keep your room clean, checking if it worked, and keeping the part that worked and changing the part that did not.

### Question 51

If you forgot a number you were supposed to write down, you would not make one up; you would go measure it again.

### Question 52

Writing yesterday's date on today's homework to make it look on time is not honest. A log must show the real day it was done.

### Question 53

You cannot sign your name on a permission slip saying you read a book you did not read. If an adult asks you to, you tell another adult.

### Question 54

The assistant is like the scorekeeper who reports the score; the coach decides what the score means and what play to call next.

### Question 55

If the scale suddenly says a much bigger number than usual, you report the real number to the grown-up instead of quietly rewriting it.

### Question 56

Before telling the teacher something looks wrong on your test, you double-check you are reading your own paper, then raise your hand.

### Question 57

If a friend says no to a game, you write 'they said no' instead of pretending they played. You record what really happened.

### Question 58

A test note is like a receipt that proves what happened; it has to be right because people may check it later.

### Question 59

If you run out of lines on your homework, you get a new sheet of paper, not write sideways in the corner.

### Question 60

It is like a teacher grading your quiz to see how well you really know the material, not just you checking your own answers.

### Question 61

When groceries arrive, you check the dates and put the cold things in the fridge, not on any shelf you find.

### Question 62

It is like checking the fridge thermometer every day so you notice the fridge is getting warm before the milk goes bad.

### Question 63

If the thermometer is broken, you do not just guess how cold the fridge is; you get a working one and tell someone to fix it.

### Question 64

It is like the scorekeeper writing the score and handing it to the coach, who then explains the score to the team.

### Question 65

If the coach asks the scorekeeper to read the score to the team, the scorekeeper reads the number but does not decide what it means.

### Question 66

An invalid result is like a blurry photo: you do not say what the photo shows; you take a new one.

### Question 67

It is like writing 'told Ms. Lee at 2:15' on a note, so later everyone knows the note was delivered and when.

### Question 68

Checking your homework after you finish is how you catch mistakes. The office checks its records the same way.

### Question 69

If every single cookie from a new batch comes out salty, you check the recipe and the ingredients, not the cookies one by one.

### Question 70

Checking one light bulb is QC; checking the whole string of lights and fixing the wiring is QA.

### Question 71

If a score is exactly at the passing line, you report the exact score and let the teacher decide, instead of bumping it up or down yourself.

### Question 72

If the smoke detector keeps failing its test, you do not keep cooking and hope for the best; you stop and get it fixed.

### Question 73

If your scale shows a very different weight than yesterday, you check the scale and step again, then tell the grown-up, instead of changing the number.

### Question 74

It is like noticing your plant is drooping, watering it, and checking the next day that it perked up — the full loop from noticing to confirming the fix.

### Question 75

If the smoke alarm goes off while you are sweeping, you stop sweeping and respond to the alarm.

### Question 76

If you put your name on the wrong paper, you fix it right away and tell the teacher, so the right paper goes to the right person.

### Question 77

An entry missing its name and batch number is like a signed note with no name on it — you cannot tell who wrote it or where it came from.

### Question 78

You retake a photo if it came out blurry, but if a clear photo shows something surprising, you show it to the grown-up instead of editing it.

### Question 79

If you see a teammate cheating on a score sheet, you tell the coach; you do not look away or join in.

### Question 80

If milk sat out all night, you would not pour it for one person and note it; you would throw it out and get fresh milk.

### Question 81

If the main teacher is absent and the alarm rings, you find the substitute teacher or the principal, and you keep trying until someone answers.

### Question 82

If the coach says to read the score to the team, you make sure you heard right and then note that you read it.

### Question 83

If an outside grader finds mistakes on your quiz, you figure out what you got wrong and practice, not hide the paper.

### Question 84

Reporting is reading the thermometer's number out loud; interpreting is deciding what that number means for the person.

### Question 85

It is like the whole recipe in order: check the oven, bake the cookies, write down how they turned out, and tell the grown-up if something looks wrong.

  "scope_note": "This bank is educational only. Waived-test documentation, result reporting, quality assurance, logging, and escalation are taught for recognition, assistance, safety, and policy-following. Whether a medical office assistant may perform a specific CLIA-waived test, and what they may document or report, depends on state law, employer policy, training, certification, and clinician delegation. Interpretation, diagnosis, and release of results to patients are always the responsibility of licensed clinicians unless the assistant is specifically authorized and delegated to communicate under office policy. When results are unusual, invalid, or critical, or when quality control fails, the correct action is always to stop, follow policy, document accurately, and escalate to qualified, authorized staff."
